{{Short description|Formula for the "volume" of an n-simplex}}

In [[linear algebra]], [[geometry]], and [[trigonometry]], the '''Cayley–Menger determinant''' is a formula for the content, i.e. the higher-dimensional [[volume]], of an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[simplex]] in terms of the squares of all the [[distance]]s between pairs of its vertices. This determinant is named after [[Arthur Cayley]] and [[Karl Menger]].

The <math>n(n+1)/2</math> pairwise distance polynomials between <math>n+1</math> points in a (real) [[Euclidean space]] are Euclidean invariants that are associated via the '''Cayley-Menger relations'''.<ref name="s1">Sitharam, Meera; St. John, Audrey; Sidman, Jessica. ''Handbook of Geometric Constraint Systems Principles''. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press. {{ISBN|978-1-4987-3891-0}}</ref> These relations served multiple purposes, such as generalising Heron's Formula, as well as computing the content of an <math>n</math>-dimensional simplex, and ultimately, in the field of [[distance geometry]], determining whether any real [[symmetric matrix]] is a Euclidean distance matrix for some <math>n+1</math> points.<ref>http://ufo2.cise.ufl.edu/index.php/Distance_Geometry Distance Geometry</ref>

== History ==
[[Karl Menger]] was a young geometry professor at the [[University of Vienna]] and [[Arthur Cayley]] was a British mathematician who specialized in [[algebraic geometry]]. Menger extended Cayley's algebraic results to propose a new axiom of [[metric space]]s using the concepts of distance geometry up to congruence equivalence, known as the Cayley–Menger determinant. This ended up generalising one of the first discoveries in [[distance geometry]], [[Heron's formula]], which computes the area of a triangle in terms of its side lengths.<ref name="s2">''[https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.02816.pdf Six Mathematical Gems from the History of Distance Geometry]''</ref>

== Definition ==
Let <math>A_0, A_1, \ldots, A_n</math> be <math>n+1</math> points in <math>k</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], with {{tmath|k \ge n}}.{{Efn|An <math>n</math>-dimensional body can't be immersed into <math>k</math>-dimensional space if {{tmath|k < n}}.}} These points are the vertices of an <math>n</math>-dimensional simplex: a triangle when {{tmath|1=n = 2}}, a [[tetrahedron]] when {{tmath|1=n = 3}}, and so on. Let <math>d_{ij}</math> be the [[Euclidean distance]]s between vertices <math>A_i</math> and {{tmath|A_j}}. The content, i.e., the <math>n</math>-dimensional volume of this simplex, denoted by {{tmath|v_n}}, can be expressed as a function of <math>n</math> and the [[determinant]] of a certain matrix, in two possible ways:<ref>{{Cite book|title=An Introduction to the Geometry of <math>n</math> Dimensions|last=Sommerville|first=D. M. Y.|publisher=Dover Publications|year=1958|location=New York}}</ref><ref name="s3">[http://mathworld.wolfram.com/Cayley-MengerDeterminant.html Cayley-Menger Determinant]'' ''</ref>

: <math display="block">
\begin{align}
{v_n}^2 & = \frac{1}{(n!)^2 2^n}
\begin{vmatrix} 
2d_{01}^2 & d_{01}^2 + d_{02}^2 - d_{12}^2 & \cdots & d_{01}^2 + d_{0n}^2 - d_{1n}^2 \\
d_{01}^2 + d_{02}^2 - d_{12}^2 & 2d_{02}^2 & \cdots & d_{02}^2 + d_{0n}^2 - d_{2n}^2 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
d_{01}^2 + d_{0n}^2 - d_{1n}^2 & d_{02}^2 + d_{0n}^2 - d_{2n}^2 & \cdots & 2d_{0n}^2
\end{vmatrix} \\[10pt]
& = \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2 2^n} 
\begin{vmatrix} 
0 & d_{01}^2 & d_{02}^2 & \cdots & d_{0n}^2 & 1 \\
d_{01}^2 & 0 & d_{12}^2 & \cdots & d_{1n}^2 & 1 \\
d_{02}^2 & d_{12}^2 & 0 & \cdots & d_{2n}^2 & 1 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
d_{0n}^2 & d_{1n}^2 & d_{2n}^2 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 & 0
\end{vmatrix}.
\end{align}
</math>

This is the '''Cayley–Menger determinant'''. For {{tmath|1=n = 2}}, we are dealing with a triangle, where swapping edges changes orientation (if orientable), but not area, thus it is necessarily a [[symmetric polynomial]] in the <math>d_{ij}</math>'s, and invariant under permutation of these quantities. For any larger n-simplex, where {{tmath|n > 2}}, only in special cases will swapping edges be invariant.{{Efn|The (hyper)volume of a figure does not depend on its vertices' numbering order.}} In particular, for {{tmath|1=n = 3}}, swapping the distances between any pair of [[skew lines|skew edges]] in a sufficiently irregular [[tetrahedron]] leads (at best) to a different tetrahedron, with a different determinant; even for the less aggressive case of swapping the distances between any pair of edges that share a vertex, this will flip the orientation of one face (formed by the three vertices of the connected edges), without flipping the orientation of their three connections to the 4th vertex, potentially forming a different tetrahedron, but this mutated object might not even be a viable tetrahedron, in the general case. 

The final row and column of <math>1</math>'s (and <math>0</math>) in the second form of this equation could simultaneously be moved to be the first row and column, giving the same result. Regardless, except for that row and column, the matrix is a [[Euclidean distance matrix]].

The usual formula for the oriented [[Simplex#Volume|volume of a simplex]] is <math>\tfrac1{n!} </math> times the determinant of the <math>n \times n</math> matrix composed of the <math>n</math> edge vectors {{tmath|A_1-A_0, \ldots, A_n-A_0}}. Unlike the Cayley–Menger determinant, the latter matrix changes with rotation of the simplex, though not with translation; regardless, its determinant and the resulting volume do not change.

== Special cases ==
To reiterate, an <math>n</math>-simplex is an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[polytope]] and the [[convex hull]] of <math>n+1</math> points which do not lie in any <math>(n-1)</math>-dimensional plane.<ref name="s6">[https://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php/Simplex Simplex ''Encyclopedia of Mathematics'']</ref>

=== <math>2</math>-Simplex ===
Hence, a <math>2</math>-simplex occurs when <math>n = 2</math> and the simplex results in a triangle. Therefore, the formula for determining <math>{v_2}^2</math> of a triangle is provided below:<ref name="s3" /><br><!--[[File:Simplex-Image.png|link=Special:FilePath/Simplex-Image.png|right|thumb|0-simplex, 1-simplex, 2-simplex, 3-simplex]]-->

<math display="block">-16 ~ {v_2}^2 = 
\begin{vmatrix}
0 & 1 & 1 & 1\\
1 & 0 & c^2 & b^2\\
1 & c^2 & 0 & a^2\\
1 & b^2 & a^2 & 0\\
\end{vmatrix}.
</math><br><!--The matrix above and the fractional formula for the simplex volume even further above are not rendering but they display correctly in this following latex server https://latexbase.com/d/38b842d7-daf7-452b-8e4a-c27dc578fa44-->

As a result, the equation above presents the content of a <math>2</math>-simplex (area of a planar triangle with side lengths {{tmath|a}}, {{tmath|b}}, and {{tmath|c}}) and it is a generalised form of Heron's Formula.<ref name="s3" />

=== <math>3</math>-Simplex ===
Similarly, a {{tmath|3}}-simplex occurs when <math>n = 3</math> and the simplex results in a tetrahedron.<ref name="s6" /> Therefore, the formula for determining <math>{v_3}^2</math> of a tetrahedron is provided below:<ref name="s3" />

<math display="block">288 ~ {v_3}^2 = 
\begin{vmatrix}
0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\\
1 & 0 & d_{12}^2 & d_{13}^2 & d_{14}^2\\
1 & d_{21}^2 & 0 & d_{23}^2 & d_{24}^2\\
1 & d_{31}^2 & d_{32}^2 & 0 & d_{34}^2\\
1 & d_{41}^2 & d_{42}^2 & d_{43}^2 & 0\\
\end{vmatrix}.
</math>

As a result, the equation above presents the content of a <math>3</math>-simplex, which is the volume of a tetrahedron where the edge between vertices <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> has length {{tmath|d_{ij} }}.<ref name="s3" />

== Proof ==
Let the column vectors <math>A_0, A_1, \ldots, A_n</math> be <math>n+1</math> points in {{tmath|n}}-dimensional Euclidean space. Starting with the volume formula in terms of an <math>(n+1) \times (n+1)</math> matrix,

<math display="block">v_n = \frac{1}{n!} \left| \det \begin{pmatrix}
A_0 & A_1 & \cdots & A_n \\
 1  &  1  & \cdots &  1
\end{pmatrix} \right|\,,</math>

we note that the determinant is unchanged when we add an extra row and column to make an <math>(n+2) \times (n+2)</math> matrix,

<math display="block">P = \begin{pmatrix}
A_0 & A_1 & \cdots & A_n & 0 \\
 1  &  1  & \cdots &  1  & 0 \\
\|A_0\|^2 & \|A_1\|^2 & \cdots & \|A_n\|^2 & 1 
\end{pmatrix}\,,</math>

where <math>\|A_j\|^2</math> is the square of the length of the vector {{tmath|A_j}}. Additionally, we note that the <math>(n+2) \times (n+2)</math> matrix

<math display="block">Q = \begin{pmatrix}
-2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -2 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & -2 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>

has a determinant of {{tmath|1=(-2)^n(-1) = (-1)^{n+1} 2^n}}. Thus,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mathpages.com/home/kmath664/kmath664.htm|title=Simplex Volumes and the Cayley–Menger Determinant|website=www.mathpages.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190516033847/https://www.mathpages.com/home/kmath664/kmath664.htm|archive-date=16 May 2019|access-date=2019-06-08}}</ref>

<math display="block">\det \begin{pmatrix} 
0 & d_{01}^2 & d_{02}^2 & \cdots & d_{0n}^2 & 1 \\
d_{01}^2 & 0 & d_{12}^2 & \cdots & d_{1n}^2 & 1 \\
d_{02}^2 & d_{12}^2 & 0 & \cdots & d_{2n}^2 & 1 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
d_{0n}^2 & d_{1n}^2 & d_{2n}^2 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
= \det(P^T Q P) = \det(Q) \det(P)^2 = (-1)^{n+1} 2^n (n!)^2 v_n^2\,.</math>

== Examples ==
In the case {{tmath|1=n = 2}}, <math>v_2</math> is the [[area]] of a [[triangle]] and thus we will denote this by {{tmath|A}}. By the Cayley–Menger determinant, where the triangle has side lengths {{tmath|a}}, {{tmath|b}}, and {{tmath|c}},

<math display="block">\begin{align}
16 A^2 &= \begin{vmatrix} 2a^2 & a^2+b^2-c^2 \\ a^2+b^2-c^2 & 2b^2 \end{vmatrix} \\[8pt]
&= 4a^2b^2 - (a^2+b^2-c^2)^2 \\[6pt]
&= (a^2+b^2+c^2)^2 - 2(a^4+b^4+c^4) \\[6pt]
&= (a+b+c)(a+b-c)(a-b+c)(-a+b+c).
\end{align}</math>

The result in the third line is due to the [[Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity|Fibonacci identity]]. The final line can be rewritten to obtain [[Heron's formula]] for the area of a triangle given its three sides, which was known to Archimedes prior.<ref>{{cite book|title=A History of Greek Mathematics (Vol II)|author=Heath, Thomas L.|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=1921|pages=321–323}}</ref>

In the case {{tmath|1=n=3}}, the quantity <math>v_3</math> gives the volume of a [[tetrahedron]], which we will denote by {{tmath|V}}. For distances between <math>A_i</math> and <math>A_j</math> denoted by {{tmath|d_{ij} }}, the Cayley–Menger determinant gives<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Audet|first=Daniel|title=Déterminants sphérique et hyperbolique de Cayley–Menger|url=https://archimede.mat.ulaval.ca/amq/bulletins/mai11/Chronique_note_math.mai11.pdf|journal=Bulletin AMQ|volume=LI|pages=45–52}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=100 Great Problems of Elementary Mathematics|url=https://archive.org/details/100greatproblems0000dorr|url-access=registration|last=Dörrie|first=Heinrich|publisher=Dover Publications|year=1965|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/100greatproblems0000dorr/page/285 285]–9}}</ref>

<math display=block>\begin{align}
144 V^2 = {} & \frac{1}{2}
\begin{vmatrix}
2d_{01}^2 & d_{01}^2+d_{02}^2-d_{12}^2 & d_{01}^2+d_{03}^2-d_{13}^2 \\
d_{01}^2+d_{02}^2-d_{12}^2 & 2d_{02}^2 & d_{02}^2+d_{03}^2-d_{23}^2 \\
d_{01}^2+d_{03}^2-d_{13}^2 & d_{02}^2+d_{03}^2-d_{23}^2 & 2d_{03}^2
\end{vmatrix} \\[8pt]
= {} & 4d_{01}^2 d_{02}^2 d_{03}^2 + (d_{01}^2+d_{02}^2-d_{12}^2)(d_{01}^2+d_{03}^2-d_{13}^2)(d_{02}^2+d_{03}^2-d_{23}^2) \\[6pt]
& {} -d_{01}^2(d_{02}^2+d_{03}^2-d_{23}^2)^2 - d_{02}^2(d_{01}^2+d_{03}^2-d_{13}^2)^2 - d_{03}^2(d_{01}^2+d_{02}^2-d_{12}^2)^2.
\end{align}</math>

=== Finding the circumradius of a simplex ===
Given a nondegenerate <math>n</math>-simplex, it has a circumscribed <math>n</math>-sphere, with radius {{tmath|r}}. Then the {{tmath|(n+1)}}-simplex made of the vertices of the {{tmath|n}}-simplex and the center of the {{tmath|n}}-sphere is degenerate. Thus, we have

<math display=block>
\begin{vmatrix} 
0 & r^2 & r^2 & r^2 & \cdots & r^2  & 1 \\
r^2 & 0 & d_{01}^2 & d_{02}^2 & \cdots & d_{0n}^2 & 1 \\
r^2 & d_{01}^2 & 0 & d_{12}^2 & \cdots & d_{1n}^2 & 1 \\
r^2 & d_{02}^2 & d_{12}^2 & 0 & \cdots & d_{2n}^2 & 1 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
r^2 & d_{0n}^2 & d_{1n}^2 & d_{2n}^2 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 & 0
\end{vmatrix} = 0\,.
</math>

Using <math>\begin{vmatrix}A & B \\ C & D\end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix}D\end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix}A - B D^{-1} C\end{vmatrix}</math>,<math>\begin{vmatrix}D\end{vmatrix} \ne 0</math>, and <math>A = \left(\begin{matrix}0\end{matrix}\right)</math>, this is equivalent to

<math display="block">
\left( \begin{matrix} r^2 & r^2 & r^2 & \cdots & r^2 & 1 \end{matrix} \right)
\left( \begin{matrix} 
0 & d_{01}^2 & d_{02}^2 & \cdots & d_{0n}^2 & 1 \\
d_{01}^2 & 0 & d_{12}^2 & \cdots & d_{1n}^2 & 1 \\
d_{02}^2 & d_{12}^2 & 0 & \cdots & d_{2n}^2 & 1 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
d_{0n}^2 & d_{1n}^2 & d_{2n}^2 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 & 0
\end{matrix} \right)^{-1}
\left( \begin{matrix} r^2 \\ r^2 \\ r^2 \\ \vdots \\ r^2 \\ 1 \end{matrix} \right)
= 0\,,
</math>
which is a [[quadratic equation]] for {{tmath|r^2}}.
Solving for {{tmath|r}}, we get <ref>{{Cite journal|last=Audet|first=Daniel|title=La courbure d’une courbe|url=https://www.amq.math.ca/wp-content/uploads/bulletin/vol58/no2/07-Note-courbure.pdf|journal=Bulletin AMQ|volume=LI|pages=61–63}}</ref>

<math display="block">
r = \left( 2 
\left( \begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \end{matrix} \right)
\left( \begin{matrix} 
0 & d_{01}^2 & d_{02}^2 & \cdots & d_{0n}^2 \\
d_{01}^2 & 0 & d_{12}^2 & \cdots & d_{1n}^2 \\
d_{02}^2 & d_{12}^2 & 0 & \cdots & d_{2n}^2 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
d_{0n}^2 & d_{1n}^2 & d_{2n}^2 & \cdots & 0
\end{matrix} \right)^{-1}
\left( \begin{matrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{matrix} \right)
\right)^{-1/2}
\,.
</math>

For example, when {{tmath|1=n = 2}}, this gives the circumradius of a triangle in terms of its edge lengths.

== Set Classifications ==
From these determinants, we also have the following classifications:

=== Straight ===
A set {{math|Λ}} (with at least three distinct elements) is called '''straight''' [[if and only if]], for any three elements {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}} of {{math|Λ}},<ref name="sFinal">[http://ufo2.cise.ufl.edu/index.php/Distance_Geometry Distance Geometry Wiki Page]</ref>

:: <math> \det \begin{bmatrix} 
       0 & d(AB)^2 & d(AC)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AB)^2 &    0    & d(BC)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AC)^2 & d(BC)^2 &       0 & 1 \\
       1 &       1 &       1 & 0
\end{bmatrix} = 0 </math>

=== Plane ===
A set {{math|Π}} (with at least four distinct elements) is called '''plane''' if and only if, for any four elements {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|C}} and {{mvar|D}} of {{math|Π}},<ref name="sFinal" />

:: <math> \det \begin{bmatrix} 
       0 & d(AB)^2 & d(AC)^2 & d(AD)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AB)^2 &    0    & d(BC)^2 & d(BD)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AC)^2 & d(BC)^2 &       0 & d(CD)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AD)^2 & d(BD)^2 & d(CD)^2 &       0 & 1 \\
       1 &       1 &       1 & 1       & 0
\end{bmatrix} = 0 </math>
but not all triples of elements of {{math|Π}} are straight to each other;

=== Flat ===
A set {{mvar|Φ}} (with at least five distinct elements) is called '''flat''' if and only if, for any five elements {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|C}}, {{mvar|D}} and {{mvar|E}} of {{mvar|Φ}},<ref name="sFinal" />

:: <math> \det \begin{bmatrix} 
       0 & d(AB)^2 & d(AC)^2 & d(AD)^2 & d(AE)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AB)^2 &    0    & d(BC)^2 & d(BD)^2 & d(BE)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AC)^2 & d(BC)^2 &       0 & d(CD)^2 & d(CE)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AD)^2 & d(BD)^2 & d(CD)^2 &       0 & d(DE)^2 & 1 \\
 d(AE)^2 & d(BE)^2 & d(CE)^2 & d(DE)^2 &       0 & 1 \\
       1 &       1 &       1 & 1       &       1 & 0
\end{bmatrix} = 0 </math>

but not all quadruples of elements of {{mvar|Φ}} are plane to each other; and so on.

== Menger's Theorem ==
Karl Menger made a further discovery after the development of the Cayley–Menger determinant, which became known as Menger's theorem (unrelated to the [[Menger's theorem|theorem of that name in graph theory]]). The theorem states:

:: For a [[finite set]] of points {{tmath|A}}, a semi-metric <math>\rho: A \times A \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq0}</math> can be obtained from a Euclidean metric of dimension n if and only if every Cayley-Menger determinant on <math>n+1</math> points is strictly positive, every determinant on <math>n+2</math> points vanishes, and a Cayley-Menger determinant on at least one set of <math>n+3</math> points is nonnegative (in which case it is necessarily zero).<ref name="s1" />

In simpler terms, if every subset of <math>n+2</math> points can be isometrically embedded in an {{tmath|n}}-dimensional, but not generally {{tmath|(n-1)}}-dimensional Euclidean space, then the semi-metric is Euclidean of dimension <math>n</math> unless <math>A</math> consists of exactly <math>n+3</math> points and the Cayley–Menger determinant on those <math>n+3</math> points is strictly negative. This type of semi-metric would be classified as ''pseudo-Euclidean''.<ref name="s1" />

== Realization of a Euclidean distance matrix ==
Given the Cayley-Menger relations as explained above, the following section will bring forth two algorithms to decide whether a given matrix is a distance matrix corresponding to a Euclidean point set. The first algorithm will do so when given a matrix AND the dimension, {{tmath|d}}, via a [http://ufo2.cise.ufl.edu/index.php/Geometric_Constraint_Solving geometric constraint solving] algorithm. The second algorithm does so when the dimension, {{tmath|d}}, is not provided. This algorithm theoretically finds a realization of the full <math>n \times n</math> Euclidean distance matrix in the smallest possible embedding dimension in quadratic time.

=== Theorem (d is given) ===
For the sake and context of the following theorem, algorithm, and example, slightly different notation will be used than before resulting in an altered formula for the volume of the <math> n-1 </math> dimensional simplex below than above.

: '''Theorem.''' An <math> n \times n </math> matrix <math> \Delta </math> is a Euclidean Distance Matrix if and only if for all <math> k \times k </math> submatrices <math> S </math> of {{tmath| \Delta }}, where {{tmath| k \leq n }}, {{tmath| \det (\hat{\delta _S}) \geq 0 }}.  For <math> \Delta </math> to have a realization in dimension {{tmath| d }}, if {{tmath|1= {{!}}S{{!}} = k \geq d + 2 }}, then {{tmath|1= \det (\hat{\delta _S}) = 0 }}.<ref name="s7">Sitharam, Meera. "Lecture 1 through 6"." Geometric Complexity CIS6930, University of Florida. Received 28 Mar.2020</ref>

As stated before, the purpose to this theorem comes from the following algorithm for realizing a Euclidean Distance Matrix or a Gramian Matrix.

==== Algorithm ====
<blockquote>
; Input
: Euclidean Distance Matrix <math> \Delta </math> or Gramian Matrix {{tmath| \Gamma }}.

; Output
: Pointset <math> P </math>

; Procedure

* If the dimension <math> d </math> is fixed, we can solve a system of polynomial equations, one for each inner product entry of {{tmath| \Gamma }}, where the variables are the coordinates of each point <math> p_1, \ldots, p_n </math> in the desired dimension {{tmath|d}}.
* Otherwise, we can solve for one point at a time.
** Solve for the coordinates of <math> p_k </math> using its distances to all previously placed points {{tmath| p_1, \ldots, p_{k-1} }}.  Thus, <math> p_k </math> is represented by at most <math> k - 1 </math> coordinate values, ensuring minimum dimension and complexity.
</blockquote>

==== Example ====
Let each point <math> p_k </math> have coordinates {{tmath| {p^1_k, p^2_k, \ldots} }}.  To place the first three points:

# Put <math> p_1 </math> at the origin, so {{tmath|1= p_1 = {0,0,\ldots} }}.
# Put <math> p_2 </math> on the first axis, so {{tmath|1= p_2 = {(\delta_{12})^2, 0, \ldots} }}.
# To place <math> p_3 </math>:

<math display=block>
\begin{cases}
(p^1_1 - p^1_3)^2 + (p^2_1 - p^2_3)^2 = (\delta_{13})^2\\
(p^1_2 - p^1_3)^2 + (p^2_2 - p^2_3)^2 = (\delta_{23})^2
\end{cases}
</math>
<math display=block>
\rightarrow
\begin{cases}
p^1_3 = \frac{(\delta_{12})^2 + (\delta_{13})^2 - (\delta_{23})^2}{2 \delta_{12}}\\
p^2_3 = \frac{\sqrt{(\delta_{31} + \delta_{32} + \delta_{12})(\delta_{31} + \delta_{32} - \delta_{12})(\delta_{31} - \delta_{32} + \delta_{12})(- \delta_{31} + \delta_{32} + \delta_{12})}}{2 \delta_{01}}
\end{cases}
</math>

In order to find a realization using the above algorithm, the [[discriminant]] of the distance quadratic system must be positive, which is equivalent to <math> \Delta p_1p_2p_3 </math> having positive volume.  In general, the volume of the <math> n-1 </math> dimensional simplex formed by the <math> n </math> vertices is given by<ref name="s7" />

<math display=block> V^{2}_{n-1} = \frac{(-1)^{n}}{2^{n-1} (n-1!)^{2}} \det (\hat{\Delta}) .</math>

In this formula above, <math>\det (\hat{\Delta}) </math> is the Cayley–Menger determinant. This volume being positive is equivalent to the determinant of the volume matrix being positive.

=== Theorem (d not given) ===
<blockquote>
Let {{mvar|K}} be a positive integer and {{mvar|D}} be a {{math|1''n'' × ''n''}} symmetric hollow matrix with nonnegative elements, with {{math|''n'' ≥ 2}}. {{mvar|D}} is a Euclidean distance matrix with {{math|1=dim(''D'') = ''K''}} if and only if there exist <math>\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K</math> and an index set {{math|1=''I'' = }}<math>\{i_1,\ldots,i_{K+1}\} \subseteq I_n </math> such that

<math display=block>\begin{cases}
  x_i = 0 \\
  x_{i_j} (j -1) \ne 0,  & \mbox{ }  j \in I_{2,K+1} \\
  x_{i_j} (i) = 0,  & \mbox{ }  j \in I_{2,K}, i \in I_{j,K},

\end{cases}
</math>

where <math>\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n</math> realizes {{mvar|D}}, where <math>x_h(l)</math> denotes the <math>l^{th}</math> component of the <math>h^{th}</math> vector.
</blockquote> 
The extensive proof of this theorem can be found at the following reference.<ref name="s8">[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0166218X18303391 Realizing Euclidean Distance Matrices by Sphere Intersection]</ref>

=== Algorithm - K = edmsph(''D'', ''x'') ===
Source:<ref name="s8" />

<math>I = \{1,2\}</math>
<math>K = 1</math>
<math>(x_1, x_2) = (0, \sqrt{D_{12}})</math>
<math>\text{for i} \in \{3,\ldots,n\}\text{ do}</math>

: Γ <math> = \bigcap_{j \in I} S^K(x_j, D_{ij})</math>
: '''if''' Γ <math> = </math> ∅; then
:: '''return''' ∞
: '''else if''' Γ <math> = \{p_i\} \text{  } then </math>
:: <math>x_i = p_i </math>
: '''else if''' Γ<math> = \{p_i^+, p_i^-\} \text{  } then </math>
:: <math> x_i = p_i^+ </math>
:: <math>x</math> ← expand(<math>x</math>)
:: {{math|''I'' ← ''I'' ∪ {{mset|''i''}}}}
:: {{math|''K'' ← ''K'' + 1}}
: '''else'''
:: '''error''': {{math|dim aff(span(''x''{{sub|''j''}})) < ''K'' - 1}}
: '''end if'''

'''end for''' 
'''return K'''
